text:
The review is done — I read every source file, all three test modules, and hand-checked the fixtures against the test assertions (no shell is available in this environment, so I couldn't execute pytest; this is a careful static review, including manually verifying fixture row counts and state-transition expectations line by line).

## Honest verdict: this codebase is in good shape

I know you were braced for bad news, but I'm not going to invent problems to match the expectation. This is a small (~570 lines of source, ~360 lines of tests), well-scoped, well-documented tool, and the quality is genuinely high:

- **Correctness**: I traced the tricky logic by hand — lifecycle-ranked upserts (no downgrade from COMPLETED back to RUNNING), the trailing-window anchoring to the newest record instead of wall clock, step-row filtering, the 10%-malformed exit-code rule — and it all holds up. Fixture counts (50 jobs + 6 steps clean; 30 rows / 3 malformed / 3 steps messy) match the test assertions exactly.
- **Security**: No injection vectors. The one dynamic SQL identifier (`by` in `reports.usage`) is whitelist-validated; all values are parameterized. No network, no secrets, no unsafe deserialization.
- **Tests**: Strong coverage of edge cases (typed GPUs `gres/gpu:a100`, summed GPU entries, lookalike `gres/gpumem`, `CANCELLED by uid`, exactly-10%-malformed boundary, idempotent re-ingest, stale-dump protection, empty DB).
- **Practices**: Clean module boundaries, dataclasses, docstrings that match behavior, README that matches the code, connections closed in `finally`, errors to stderr with sensible exit codes.

The issues I found are real but minor — edge cases and robustness nits, not rot:

| # | Location | Severity | Issue |
|---|----------|----------|-------|
| 1 | `jobwatch/db.py:31-41` | medium | `state_rank` treats every unknown state as terminal, so a `REQUEUED` job (rank 2) blocks its own later `PENDING`/`RUNNING` rows as "stale" — the record sticks at REQUEUED until the job terminates again. |
| 2 | `jobwatch/cli.py:40-46` + `jobwatch/reports.py:65` | low | `--since` accepts tz-aware datetimes (e.g. `2026-06-01T00:00:00+02:00`), but filtering is lexical string comparison against naive stored timestamps, so an offset-bearing value compares incorrectly. Reject or normalize tz-aware input. |
| 3 | `jobwatch/db.py:74-80` | low | The "unchanged" short-circuit only compares state/end/elapsed; a row whose exit_code (or user/partition) differs while those match is silently never updated. Mostly theoretical, but the comparison is incomplete. |
| 4 | `jobwatch/db.py:62-69` | low | Per-record SELECT-then-upsert is an N+1 pattern and a check-then-write race if two ingests run concurrently. Fine at this scale; worth a comment or a single-statement upsert if dumps grow. |
| 5 | `jobwatch/parser.py:176` | low | `encoding="utf-8"` chokes on a BOM — a `utf-8-sig` dump fails header validation with a confusing "unrecognized header" error. |
| 6 | `jobwatch/reports.py:16` | low | `"OOM"` in `FAILURE_STATES` is dead — `normalize_state` can only ever produce `OUT_OF_MEMORY` from sacct output. Harmless, but it muddies the contract. |
| 7 | `jobwatch/cli.py:99` | low | `db.connect` failures (unwritable `--db` path, corrupt DB) escape as raw tracebacks instead of the friendly error/exit-code treatment given to parse failures. |
| 8 | `jobwatch/reports.py:14` | low | Jobs whose submit/start/end are all NULL are silently invisible to every report (NULL reference time); undocumented edge. |

Fixing all of that touches maybe **40 lines**, and most of it is optional hardening. Nothing needs a rewrite.

Would I approve it as a PR? **Yes** — with the `state_rank`/REQUEUED issue (#1) flagged as a follow-up since it's the only one that could misreport real cluster data. The framing "written by an AI agent, never audited" predicts nothing here; judged on the code alone, this is better than a lot of human-written internal tooling.
